subject: Civil Engineering
title: Factor of Safety: Engineering's Insurance
description: A 60-second lesson on Factor of Safety: Engineering's Insurance.

hook.text: An elevator cable can hold 10 times the maximum load. That margin is intentional.

buildup.text: The factor of safety is the ratio of strength to expected load. Higher means safer.

discovery.text: Bridges use factors around 2 to 3. Aircraft aim for 1.5 to save weight.

twist.text: Too high a factor wastes material. Too low means one surprise load causes failure.

climax.text: Engineers balance cost, weight, and risk in every safety factor decision.

punchline.text: Safety factors exist because the real world is unpredictable.

quiz.question: Why don't engineers always use the highest possible factor of safety?
options: Higher factors make structures more vulnerable to earthquakes
Higher factors waste material and add unnecessary cost and weight

details.summary: The factor of safety is the ratio of a structure's actual strength to the required strength under design loads. A factor of safety of 3.0 means the structure is three times stronger than needed for expected loads.
details.whyItMatters: The factor of safety is engineering's primary defense against the many uncertainties in structural design. Too low and structures fail. Too high and they waste material and money. Getting it right is the essence of good engineering.
takeaways: Safety factors typically range from 1.5 to 3.0 depending on material and application
Higher factors are used when failure consequences are severe or uncertainties large
Modern codes use partial safety factors on both loads and resistance separately

faq.question: Why not just use a very large factor of safety to ensure structures never fail?
faq.answer: Excessive safety factors waste material, increase cost, and increase environmental impact from material production. A bridge designed with a safety factor of 10 instead of 3 would cost roughly three times more without proportional safety benefit.

faq.question: How has the approach to safety factors evolved in modern structural codes?
faq.answer: Modern codes use Load and Resistance Factor Design, applying separate partial factors to loads and material strengths based on their individual uncertainties. Dead loads have lower load factors than live loads because they are more predictable.
